builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Capability Gain from ISA to Shared Execution on AMD MI300A and MI250X
summary: Replaces ad-hoc peak-throughput comparisons with a metric tracing instruction-level gains through libraries, applications, and shared queues, applied to AMD MI300A vs MI250X. Requires CDNA3 hardware with FP8 and 2:4 sparse instructions plus vendor-library support; quantization must be fused into GEMMs to avoid overhead. Fails in production when unfused quantization makes FP8 a per-layer slowdown in LLM inference, when sparsity library support captures only half the theoretical gain, and when queue-shared serving gains nothing from lower precision.
rationale: The findings require AMD MI300A hardware unavailable to a reader on one 24 GB GPU or third-party APIs, so the method is informative but not directly adoptable.
technique: Capability-gain analysis of MI300A FP8 and 2:4 sparsity

claims.statement: Replaces ad-hoc peak-throughput comparisons with a metric tracing instruction-level gains through libraries, applications, and shared queues, applied to AMD MI300A vs MI250X. Requires CDNA3 hardware with FP8 and 2:4 sparse instructions plus vendor-library support; quantization must be fused into GEMMs to avoid overhead. Fails in production when unfused quantization makes FP8 a per-layer slowdown in LLM inference, when sparsity library support captures only half the theoretical gain, and when queue-shared serving gains nothing from lower precision.
FP8 retains most of its instruction-level speedup through hipBLASLt on an 8192^3 GEMM relative to MI250X FP16, and 2:4 sparsity keeps at most about half of its speedup in hipSPARSELt.
